nameStory: The Circumpolar Eualid gets its name from its incredible geographic range — it's found all around the Arctic and northern regions of the world, literally 'circling the pole.' The genus name Eualus comes from Greek meaning 'well-jointed,' referring to the distinctly segmented bodies that make these tiny shrimp so recognizable under a magnifying glass.
description: The Circumpolar Eualid is a tiny marine shrimp that lives in the cold waters off New England's coast. These translucent creatures are only about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long, making them easy to overlook despite being fairly common. They have the classic shrimp body plan with a curved back, long antennae, and multiple pairs of swimming legs underneath. Their bodies are mostly clear with subtle orange or reddish tints, especially visible in the eggs that females carry.

idTips.label: Size and transparency
idTips.description: Extremely small at 0.5-0.75 inches long with a glassy, nearly transparent body that feels delicate and slippery when gently handled

idTips.label: Rostrum shape
idTips.description: The pointed beak-like projection (rostrum) between the eyes has 3-7 small teeth on top and extends well beyond the eyes

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Body appears clear to pale with subtle orange, pink, or reddish highlights, particularly noticeable in egg-bearing females

idTips.label: Swimming behavior
idTips.description: Moves with quick, jerky swimming motions using rapid beats of their paddle-like swimmerets under the curved abdomen

idTips.label: Antenna length
idTips.description: Two pairs of very long, thread-like antennae that extend well beyond the body length and feel bristly to the touch

habitat: Found in cold, deeper waters along New England's rocky coastlines, typically at depths of 30-300 feet where the water stays consistently cold year-round. They prefer areas with good water circulation around rocky bottoms, kelp beds, and areas where organic matter settles. Most commonly encountered by divers or in research trawls rather than in tide pools.

seasonality.spring: Active in deeper waters as females begin carrying bright orange egg masses that are visible through their transparent bodies.
seasonality.summer: Peak reproductive season when egg-bearing females are most commonly observed, though they remain in deeper, cooler waters.
seasonality.fall: Young shrimp begin appearing in samples as the new generation matures, often found in slightly shallower waters than adults.
seasonality.winter: Adults retreat to deepest parts of their range where water temperatures remain stable above freezing.

funFact: Despite being tiny, these shrimp are incredibly hardy Arctic survivors — the same species you might find off Maine's coast also lives in the frigid waters around Greenland, Norway, and Alaska, making them one of the most cold-adapted shrimp in the world.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other tiny transparent shrimp in New England waters, but the Circumpolar Eualid's distinctly toothed rostrum (beak) and extremely small size help distinguish it. Remember: if it's smaller than your thumbnail and has a spiky nose, you've likely found a eualid shrimp.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'eualid' is unfamiliar to most people because these creatures are rarely encountered except by marine biologists and deep-water fishermen. They're part of the same group as the shrimp you might eat, but their tiny size and deep-water habitat keep them off dinner plates and out of most field guides.
compareHints: The Circumpolar Eualid is larger and more robust than its relative the Doll Eualid, which is even tinier at less than half an inch long. The Circumpolar species also tends to have more pronounced rostral teeth and slightly more colorful markings. Both species require magnification to identify with certainty, but the Circumpolar Eualid's greater size makes it the more likely species to be noticed by casual observers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Doll Eualids are much smaller than their relative the Circumpolar Eualid, which can grow to over an inch long.
